newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Relatives ask Kashmir group to help find hostages.
newsitem.headline: Relatives ask Kashmir group to help find hostages.

text.p: Relatives and friends of Western tourists abducted nearly two years ago in the Indian-ruled part of disputed Kashmir appealed to a militant group on Friday to help find the hostages.

They told a news conference in Muzaffarabad, capital of the one-third of Kashmir under Pakistan control, that previous appeals by the Harkat-ul-Ansar guerrilla group for the release of the hostages were not enough and it should do more.
"We want them to help us to know about their (hostages') whereabouts," said Julie Mangan, wife of Keith Mangan, one of two Britons among the hostages.
"We don't know what is happening or what has happened to the hostages," she said.

Britons Paul Wells and Keith Mangan were abducted by the shadowy Al-Faran guerrilla group while trekking through the Himalayas in July 1995. German Dirk Hasert, Norwegian Hans Christian Ostroe and Americans Donald Hutchings and John Childs were also captured.
Childs escaped and Ostroe was later found beheaded. There has been no trace of the other four for 16 months, raising doubts over whether they are still alive.
India links Harkat to the kidnapping. But the group denies any involvement in the kidnapping or links with Al-Faran, and issued its own appeal 10 days ago for the hostages' release.

"We did have proof to say that Harkat-ul-Ansar was behind the Al-Faran in the beginning," said Julie Mangan. "Now Al-Faran was a splinter group of Harkat-ul-Ansar, so we look upon them (Harkat) to help us to find the answers."
Mangan was accompanied by Paul Wells' father Bob Wells, and Paul's girlfriend Catherine Mosley, and a cousin of her own.

The group, which had arrived after a visit to India, also issued an appeal at the main mosque in Muzaffarabad after the traditional Friday congregation, urging people to come forward with any information they might have about the hostages.
Several Moslem militant groups are fighting Indian rule over two-thirds of Kashmir, the remaining third of which is controlled by Pakistan.
Wells said in New Delhi on Thursday that the group would also ask the Pakistani government's Inter-Services Intelligence wing to search for the hostages.
On Thursday, Israeli psychic Uri Geller put up a $50,000 reward for the release of the Western hostages and offered to act as an intermediary with the guerrillas who seized them.
